WRM PRO security review checklist (used by the Claude security review workflow and by the
wrm-security-review skill in .claude/skills/). WRM is a self-hosted web app that holds SSH,
RDP/VNC and BMC credentials and opens terminals on company servers, so a bug in it can hand an
attacker those servers. Review the change against these points in addition to the usual ones.

Trust boundaries and who the attacker can be:
- no account (sign-in page, share links, incoming webhooks under /api/hooks/, MCP OAuth endpoints);
- a guest of a link share, a share member with a low role (observer, viewer);
- a signed-in user who is not an administrator (must never reach another user's connections,
  credentials, sessions, recordings, AI transcripts or MCP tokens);
- an AI model or MCP client acting for a user (its output and the server output it reads are
  untrusted input: prompt injection);
- text and files coming from managed servers (terminal output, file names, Git repositories,
  deploy-config YAML, imports from mRemoteNG / CSV / XLSX / SSH config).

Check in particular:
1. Authorization: every new or changed /api/ handler calls requireAuth or requireAdmin (or the
   share/role check) and scopes every database query to the user (user_id / owner_id) or to a
   share role that allows the action (roleCan). Look for IDs taken from the request and used
   without an ownership check (IDOR).
2. Sessions and CSRF: state-changing requests keep going through securityMiddleware (X-WRM-Request
   header and same-origin check); no new exception besides /api/hooks/ without a secret check.
   Restricted sessions (must change password, must set up 2FA) only reach restrictedAllowedPaths.
3. Secrets: passwords, private keys, tokens and TOTP secrets are stored with encryptValue, never
   returned to the browser, never written to logs, and audit details use neutral keys (cred_id),
   because keys containing password/token/credential/private_key are redacted.
4. Command execution: commands run on remote servers or locally (exec.Command, SSH sessions,
   Docker, PowerShell) must not be built by concatenating untrusted text into a shell string;
   arguments are passed as separate argv items or quoted with the existing helpers.
5. Paths: file names from requests, archives (ZIP/tar bundles), imports or remote servers must not
   escape their directory (.., absolute paths, symlinks, Windows drive letters and UNC paths).
6. Outbound requests: URLs supplied by users (Git sources, AI providers, NetBox, Redfish/BMC,
   notification webhooks) can reach internal networks; check that new ones are limited to who
   may configure them and that TLS verification is only skipped where the user chose it.
7. Browser: the UI is inline JavaScript with a CSP that allows inline scripts, so any HTML built
   from server, terminal, file, share-chat or AI text without escaping is a stored XSS with the
   full power of the session. Check innerHTML / insertAdjacentHTML with such values.
8. AI and MCP: new tools respect the user's AI policy (read_only / ask / auto, ai_full_access,
   ai_blocked_commands, ai_read_deny_paths, sensitive reads) and ask for approval before changes;
   MCP tokens are checked for scope, expiry and a disabled account.
9. Audit: security-relevant actions write an audit entry (auditLog / auditLogRef); the audit
   table stays append-only.
10. Database: migrations stay additive (CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN); SQL
    uses placeholders for values; table or column names are never taken from requests.
11. Limits: request bodies, uploads, archives and decompression have size limits.

Report only problems with a concrete path from one of the attackers above to the impact. Name
the attacker, the request or input, and the effect.
